result: The authors demonstrate that the chemotaxis complex and flagellar motor colocalize at the same cell pole in P. aeruginosa. Using fluorescence microscopy with CheY-eYFP fusion proteins and flagellar filament labeling, they observed that 145 cells with labeled flagella all exhibited consistent colocalization of the chemotaxis complex and flagellum at the same pole.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer sa0 states the data is 'convincing' that 'the chemotaxis complex and the flagella - colocalize to the same pole.' Reviewer sa2 confirms 'It is clear that the motor and receptors co-localize.' Reviewer sa3 notes the authors 'found that flagella and chemosensory clusters always co-localize in the cell.' No concerns were raised about this core observation.

result: The authors claim that FlhF controls the distribution pattern of both the chemotaxis complex and flagellar motor. In ΔflhF mutants, the chemotaxis complex no longer localizes robustly at the cell pole (with a 12.8% decrease in precise polar distribution), and the flagellar motor assembly positions change accordingly while maintaining colocalization with the chemotaxis complex. The authors conclude that FlhF has minimal impact on assembly efficiency but affects unipolar distribution.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer sa3 explicitly states the authors 'discovered that a certain protein (FlhF) is required for the polar localization of the chemosensory cluster.' Reviewer sa2 notes 'FlhF is involved in localizing the receptors and motor to the cell pole, but a separate mechanism colocalizes them.' The data showing maintained colocalization in ΔflhF mutants (101 cells observed) and the quantitative decrease in polar distribution are not questioned.

result: The authors demonstrate that the efficient assembly of the chemoreceptor cluster is partially dependent on the integrity of the motor structure. In ΔfliG and ΔfliF mutants (which disrupt motor assembly), the proportion of cells with obvious chemoreceptor clusters decreased significantly (59.8% and 62.5% respectively, compared to ~90% in wild-type). Western blotting confirmed that CheY expression levels were similar across strains, indicating the effect is due to structural integrity rather than expression changes.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer sa3 explicitly states the authors 'discovered that...core motor structures are necessary for the assembly of the cluster.' The data quality is affirmed by reviewer sa2 who notes 'The experiments and data are high quality.' The Western blot controls addressing expression levels are not challenged, and the conclusion that motor structural integrity affects chemotaxis complex assembly is accepted.

result: The authors discovered that overexpression of CheY leads to high intracellular levels of c-di-GMP and triggers cell aggregation. Using a c-di-GMP monitoring system, they found that CheY overexpression increased c-di-GMP levels by 71.8% compared to wild-type, while cheY deletion decreased levels by 58.6%. Higher inducer concentrations produced more pronounced cell aggregation, and co-expression of a phosphodiesterase (PDE) mitigated the aggregation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer sa2 explicitly states 'elevated CheY levels lead to elevated c-di-GMP' and notes 'The experiments and data are high quality.' The connection between CheY overexpression, c-di-GMP elevation, and cell aggregation is not challenged. The PDE rescue experiment providing additional support for the mechanism is not questioned.

result: The authors conclude that the colocalization of the chemoreceptor cluster and flagellum in P. aeruginosa serves to avoid cross-pathway signaling interference, enabling cells to conduct various physiological activities in an orderly manner. They propose that CheY-P can accomplish threshold-limited cross-pathway regulation, and that spatial integration ensures robust existence while preventing mutual interference with collateral pathways.
evaluation: Reviewers find this interpretation plausible. Reviewer sa2 explicitly states 'The signaling crosstalk argument is plausible.' Reviewer sa3 notes the work 'enhances our understanding of the subtlety of interaction between the chemosensory cluster and the flagellar motor to regulate cell motility.' While this is an interpretive conclusion rather than direct observation, reviewers accept the logic connecting the colocalization data to the functional significance of avoiding pathway interference.

result: The authors present supporting data on chemotaxis complex assembly efficiency across various mutants. They report that ~90% of wild-type cells contain obvious receptor clusters, >80% of ΔflhF cells contain clusters, the stator mutant (ΔmotAΔmotCD) performed similarly to wild-type (84.3%), and the ΔflhFΔfliF double mutant showed ~50% with obvious clusters. Western blotting confirmed similar CheY expression across strains, and the ΔcheA mutant showed no effect on flagellar assembly.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these supporting quantitative measurements without challenge. Reviewer sa1 notes 'the results are convincing' and reviewer sa2 states 'The experiments and data are high quality.' The Western blot controls and reciprocal experiments (showing chemotaxis complex deletion doesn't affect motor assembly) strengthen the conclusions and are not questioned by reviewers.

result: The authors describe their methodological approach using flagellar filament labeling through sulfhydryl-maleimide conjugation (with FliCT394C cysteine mutation) and cheY-eyfp fusion with a 3x glycine linker to visualize chemotaxis complex positions. They validated that CheY-EYFP accurately marks the chemoreceptor complex location by showing high spatial overlap with CheA-CFP.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodology without challenge. Reviewer sa1 notes the authors 'applied multiple techniques to study the bacterial motility system including fluorescence light microscopy and gene editing' and that 'the work can now be regarded as complete.' The validation of CheY-EYFP as an accurate marker through colocalization with CheA-CFP is not questioned.

result: The authors describe the cell division pattern in P. aeruginosa, observing that before cell division, both poles of the mother cell assemble chemotaxis complexes and flagellar motors. As the cell matures and elongates, a new flagellum grows at the opposing pole accompanied by assembly of a fresh chemotaxis complex, ensuring daughter cells possess complete motility and chemotaxis capabilities.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this observational description of the cell cycle pattern. Reviewer sa1 states 'the results are convincing, the conclusions are justified' and reviewer sa3 notes the manuscript is 'clearly-written and straightforward.' The cell division observations supporting the construction mode model are not challenged.
